title: Space radiation
summary: Outside the protection of Earth's atmosphere and magnetic field, crews receive more radiation than on the ground.
details: Two main sources: galactic cosmic rays (constant, high energy) and solar particle events (sudden bursts from the Sun).
Long-term concerns studied by NASA include cancer risk and effects on the central nervous system and the cardiovascular system.
Protection comes from shielding, storm shelters inside the spacecraft, monitoring and limiting exposure time.
NOVA MEDICA cannot measure radiation. It only helps you notice general health changes.

title: Isolation and confinement
summary: A small crew in a small space for months affects mood, sleep and teamwork.
details: Typical effects are anxiety, irritability, low motivation and poor sleep.
Mood often changes before other health problems appear, so a daily check-in is useful.
Helpful habits: regular schedule, exercise, private time, contact with family and friends, honest talk with crewmates.

title: Distance from Earth
summary: On the way to Mars, help from Earth is slow and a quick return is impossible.
details: Radio signals to Mars take up to about 20 minutes one way, so a live conversation with a doctor is not possible.
Crews must be able to act on their own: clear instructions, a stocked medical kit and offline tools.
This is why NOVA MEDICA works without internet and prepares a summary for the doctor on Earth.

title: Altered gravity
summary: Microgravity and low-gravity environments change how the body works.
details: Body fluids shift toward the head: facial puffiness, pressure changes and possible vision changes.
Without regular exercise, bones and muscles lose strength.
The heart and blood vessels adapt, and some people feel dizzy when gravity returns.
Daily exercise is part of the crew's routine for this reason.

title: Hostile and closed environment
summary: Air, water, noise and microbes in a sealed spacecraft all affect health.
details: Raised CO2 can cause headache and sleepiness, and poor air quality can lower SpO2.
Germs spread easily in a small shared space.
Noise, light cycles and temperature also affect sleep and mood.
Cabin air alarms are the first thing to check if several crew members feel unwell.

title: Bone and muscle loss
summary: Without gravity loading, bones and muscles weaken during long missions.
details: Weight-bearing bones can lose density at a rate of around one percent per month in microgravity.
Resistance and aerobic exercise, nutrition and medical monitoring reduce the loss.
Recovery after return takes time and is not always complete.

title: Immune system changes
summary: Stress, radiation, disturbed sleep and confinement can change how the immune system responds.
details: Crews sometimes show dormant viruses becoming active again and changes in immune cells.
A fever is a reason to measure again, rest and tell the flight surgeon.
Good sleep, nutrition and hygiene help.

title: Cardiovascular changes
summary: The heart and blood vessels adapt to spaceflight, and long-term radiation exposure may add risk.
details: Resting heart rate and blood pressure can shift because fluids move toward the upper body.
Compare your values with your own baseline, not only with Earth norms.
Chest pain, fainting or a very fast or slow pulse need urgent medical advice.
